subject: biology
title: Unit 4 practice exam
summary: A timed, exam-style test of all of Unit 4: six short-answer questions (40 marks) with full worked solutions, plus 20 multiple-choice questions on immunity, disease, evolution, speciation, fossils and phylogeny.
body:
This practice exam covers all of VCE Biology Unit 4, set out like the end-of-year exam: written questions that ask you to explain, apply and analyse data, plus multiple-choice questions. Taking it under real conditions shows you which topics are secure and which need more work before the exam.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time:** allow **60 minutes**: about 20 minutes for the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 40 minutes for the short-answer section (40 marks). That is about one mark per minute, the pace of the real exam.
- **Conditions:** work alone without notes, textbook or phone. A basic calculator is allowed.
- **Order:** you may start with either section, but keep to time.
- **Marking:** write full answers on paper, then mark them strictly against the worked solutions. Award a mark only when your answer contains the idea the solution credits.
- **Afterwards:** note each topic where you lost marks, revise that lesson, and redo those questions a few days later.

## Topics covered

- Pathogens, self and non-self, MHC markers and the first line of defence
- The innate immune response: inflammation, innate cells, complement, interferons, fever, lymphatic system
- Adaptive immunity: antigen presentation, clonal selection, humoral and cell-mediated responses
- Vaccines, types of immunity, herd immunity and monoclonal antibodies
- Emerging and re-emerging diseases, zoonoses and outbreak control
- Genetic change in populations: selection, drift, gene flow, antibiotic resistance
- Speciation and isolating mechanisms
- Fossils, relative and radiometric dating
- Structural and molecular evidence and phylogenetic trees
- Human evolution
- Scientific investigation methods

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (8 marks)

A child cuts her knee on a rusty fence. Bacteria enter the wound. Within a few hours, the area is red, warm and swollen.

a. Name one part of the first line of defence that was breached and explain how it normally protects the body. (2 marks)

b. Explain how mast cells cause the redness and swelling seen around the cut. (3 marks)

c. Describe how neutrophils reach the site and what they do there. (2 marks)

d. Two days later, a dendritic cell from the wound arrives in a nearby lymph node. Explain why this is important. (1 mark)

### Question 2 (8 marks)

A person is infected with a virus for the first time. The table below shows the concentration of antibody against the virus in their blood.

| Day after first infection | Antibody level (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 7 | 5 |
| 14 | 40 |
| 21 | 15 |

The same person is exposed to the same virus again on day 120. By day 127, their antibody level is 300 units.

a. Explain why antibody levels did not rise until about a week after first infection. (2 marks)

b. Explain why the response after day 120 is faster and larger. (2 marks)

c. Antibodies cannot destroy virus particles that are already inside cells. Describe how the immune system eliminates infected cells. (3 marks)

d. Explain why a person with very few helper T cells would have a poor antibody response. (1 mark)

### Question 3 (6 marks)

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. In recent years, measles cases have increased in some countries where vaccination rates have fallen.

a. Explain how the measles vaccine provides long-term protection. (2 marks)

b. Explain what herd immunity is and why falling vaccination rates allow measles to spread. (2 marks)

c. Is measles in these countries an emerging or a re-emerging disease? Justify your answer. (1 mark)

d. A baby too young to be vaccinated has some protection against measles from its mother. Name this type of immunity. (1 mark)

### Question 4 (7 marks)

Scientists studied a population of mosquitoes in a region where the insecticide DDT was sprayed. Before spraying, 2% of mosquitoes carried an allele (R) giving resistance to DDT. After several years of spraying, 75% of mosquitoes carried R.

a. Explain how the frequency of allele R increased, using the process of natural selection. (4 marks)

b. In a sample of 500 mosquitoes, 180 were RR, 220 were Rr and 100 were rr. Calculate the frequency of allele R. Show your working. (2 marks)

c. Explain why the resistance allele must have been present before spraying began. (1 mark)

### Question 5 (6 marks)

Two populations of a ground-dwelling beetle once formed a single population. A river changed course and split them. After many thousands of years, beetles from the two sides were brought together but did not produce fertile offspring.

a. Name the type of speciation that occurred. (1 mark)

b. Explain how the two populations became separate species. (4 marks)

c. Give one example of a post-zygotic isolating mechanism that could be operating. (1 mark)

### Question 6 (5 marks)

A fossil skull was found in a sedimentary rock layer between two volcanic ash layers. The lower ash layer was dated at 2.1 million years and the upper ash layer at 1.8 million years.

a. Give the age range of the fossil and explain why scientists dated the ash layers rather than the fossil itself. (2 marks)

b. The foramen magnum of the skull is positioned centrally beneath the skull. What does this suggest about the organism? Explain. (2 marks)

c. Explain why carbon-14 could not be used to date this fossil. (1 mark)

## Worked solutions

### Question 1

a. The **skin** (intact skin) (1 mark). It is a physical barrier of tightly packed, keratinised dead cells that pathogens cannot easily cross; its sebum and acidity also discourage growth (1 mark).

b. Damaged tissue triggers **mast cells** to release **histamine** (1 mark). Histamine causes **vasodilation** of local arterioles, increasing blood flow, which causes redness and warmth (1 mark). It also makes capillary walls **more permeable**, so fluid and proteins leak into the tissue, causing swelling (1 mark).

c. Cells at the site release **chemokines**, and neutrophils move towards them by **chemotaxis**, squeezing out of the leaky capillaries (1 mark). Neutrophils engulf and destroy the bacteria by **phagocytosis** (1 mark).

d. The dendritic cell **presents antigen on MHC class II** to helper T cells in the lymph node, starting the specific adaptive response. (1 mark)

### Question 2

a. This is a **primary response**. Only a few B cells have receptors matching the antigen. They must be found and activated (**clonal selection**) and then divide and differentiate into **plasma cells** (**clonal expansion**) before large amounts of antibody are made, which takes time (2 marks: selection and expansion idea 1, plasma cells producing antibodies 1).

b. The first infection produced **memory B cells** (1 mark). On re-exposure, these are already present in large numbers and are rapidly activated to form plasma cells, producing more antibody, sooner (1 mark).

c. Infected cells display viral antigen on **MHC class I** (1 mark). **Cytotoxic T cells** with the matching receptor (activated with the help of cytokines from helper T cells) bind to these cells (1 mark) and release **perforin and granzymes**, causing the infected cell to undergo **apoptosis**, so the virus cannot finish replicating (1 mark).

d. Helper T cells release **cytokines** needed to activate B cells to divide and become plasma cells, so few antibodies would be made. (1 mark)

### Question 3

a. The vaccine contains a weakened (live attenuated) form of the virus that triggers a primary response without causing disease (1 mark). This produces **memory cells**, which give a rapid secondary response if the real virus is encountered (1 mark).

b. **Herd immunity** occurs when a high enough proportion of the population is immune that the pathogen cannot pass from person to person, protecting those who are not immune (1 mark). When vaccination rates fall, there are more non-immune people, so chains of transmission are no longer broken and the virus spreads (1 mark).

c. **Re-emerging**: measles was previously controlled but is now increasing again. (1 mark)

d. **Natural passive immunity** (antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk). (1 mark)

### Question 4

a. Model answer (1 mark each):
- There was **variation** in the population: a few mosquitoes carried the R allele, which arose by random mutation.
- DDT spraying acted as a **selection pressure**, killing most mosquitoes without R.
- Mosquitoes with R were more likely to **survive and reproduce**.
- They passed the R allele to their offspring, so over many generations the **frequency of R in the gene pool increased**.

b. Copies of R = (2 × 180) + 220 = 360 + 220 = 580 (1 mark). Total alleles = 2 × 500 = 1000. Frequency of R = 580 ÷ 1000 = **0.58** (1 mark).

c. Mutations arise **randomly**; DDT did not cause the mutation, it only selected for mosquitoes that already had it. (1 mark)

### Question 5

a. **Allopatric speciation**. (1 mark)

b. Model answer (1 mark each):
- The river acted as a **geographical barrier**, stopping **gene flow** between the two populations.
- Each population experienced different **mutations** and possibly **genetic drift**.
- Different environmental **selection pressures** on each side favoured different alleles, so **allele frequencies** changed independently.
- Over a long time, the gene pools became so different that the populations were **reproductively isolated**: they could no longer produce fertile offspring, so they are separate species.

c. Any one: **hybrid sterility** (offspring are infertile), hybrid inviability (offspring die early), hybrid breakdown (later generations are weak or infertile). (1 mark)

### Question 6

a. Between **1.8 and 2.1 million years** old (1 mark). Sedimentary rock is made of fragments of older rock, so it cannot be dated reliably by radiometric methods; volcanic ash forms at one time and can be dated (for example with potassium-40) (1 mark).

b. The organism was **bipedal** (walked upright on two legs) (1 mark). A central foramen magnum means the spinal cord entered from directly below, so the head was balanced on top of a vertical spine (1 mark).

c. The fossil is far older than about 50 000 years, so almost no carbon-14 would remain to measure (and the original organic material has likely been replaced by minerals). (1 mark)

## Summary

- Use about one minute per mark and write in full sentences with key terms (histamine, MHC I, clonal selection, selection pressure, gene flow).
- Explanations earn marks when they link steps: cause, mechanism, effect.
- In calculations, show working: allele frequency = copies of the allele ÷ total alleles; age = half-lives × half-life.
- For evolution and speciation answers, always mention variation, the barrier or selection pressure, and the change in allele frequencies.
- After marking, revise the lessons behind every lost mark and retry the questions later.

questions.prompt: Which feature would allow a scientist to identify a pathogen as a bacterium rather than a fungus?

options.C: It can cause disease in humans.
options.D: It contains DNA.

questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus; fungi are eukaryotes. Option A is tempting, but both bacteria and fungi have cell walls (fungal walls are made of chitin).

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a chemical barrier in the first line of defence?

options.C: Normal flora on the skin
options.D: Phagocytosis by neutrophils

questions.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls, a chemical barrier. Option B is a physical barrier, option C is microbiological, and option D is part of the second line of defence.

questions.prompt: Plants defend themselves against fungal entry in several ways. Which is a physical barrier?

options.C: A thick, waxy cuticle on leaves
options.D: Producing antibodies

questions.explanation: A waxy cuticle physically blocks entry. Option A is a chemical barrier. Option D is wrong because plants do not make antibodies.

questions.prompt: Interferons protect the body against viruses by

options.A: binding directly to virus particles in the blood.
options.B: signalling nearby cells to increase their resistance to viral replication.
options.C: causing vasodilation at the infection site.
options.D: activating B cells to make antibodies.

questions.explanation: Infected cells release interferons, which warn neighbouring cells so they can resist viral replication. Option A is tempting, but interferons do not bind and neutralise viruses; that is what antibodies do.

questions.prompt: Which statement about complement proteins is correct?

options.A: They are made by plasma cells and are specific to one antigen.
options.B: They are released by mast cells to cause inflammation.
options.C: They are found only in lymph nodes.
options.D: They can coat pathogens to enhance phagocytosis and form pores that lyse pathogens.

questions.explanation: Complement proteins circulate in the blood and act through opsonisation, chemotaxis and lysis. Option A is tempting because antibodies can activate complement, but complement itself is non-specific and part of innate immunity.

questions.prompt: Where does clonal selection of lymphocytes mainly occur?

options.C: At the site of the cut
options.D: In the bloodstream

questions.explanation: Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes, where the matching lymphocytes are selected and expanded. Option B is tempting because T cells mature in the thymus, but maturation is not the same as activation by antigen.

questions.prompt: The variable region of an antibody

options.A: is the same in all antibodies made by a person.
options.B: binds to MHC class II markers.
options.C: forms the antigen-binding site that fits a specific epitope.
options.D: attaches the antibody to phagocytes only.

questions.explanation: The variable regions at the tips of the Y differ between antibodies and give each one its specificity for a particular epitope. Option A describes the constant region, which is similar across antibodies of the same class.

questions.prompt: HIV destroys helper T cells. Which consequence is most likely?

options.A: Only the humoral response is affected.
options.B: Only the innate response is affected.
options.C: There is no effect because cytotoxic T cells can work alone.
options.D: Both humoral and cell-mediated responses are weakened.

questions.explanation: Helper T cells release cytokines needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so losing them weakens both branches. Option C is tempting, but cytotoxic T cells need helper T cell signals for full activation and expansion.

questions.prompt: Which vaccine type contains an inactivated bacterial toxin?

options.C: Live attenuated vaccine
options.D: Viral vector vaccine

questions.explanation: A toxoid is a toxin treated so it is harmless but still antigenic, used for diseases such as tetanus. Option C is tempting, but live attenuated vaccines contain whole weakened pathogens, not toxins.

questions.prompt: A monoclonal antibody used to treat rheumatoid arthritis binds and blocks the cytokine TNF. The aim of this treatment is to

options.A: boost the immune attack on joint tissue.
options.B: reduce inflammation driven by the immune system.
options.C: give the patient lasting active immunity.
options.D: kill cancer cells in the joint.

questions.explanation: In autoimmune disease the immune system attacks self tissue, so blocking an inflammatory cytokine reduces damage. Option C is wrong because monoclonal antibodies give passive immunity with no memory, so treatment must be repeated.

questions.prompt: A new influenza strain appears suddenly after two different strains infect the same pig and exchange whole gene segments. This is

options.C: antigenic shift.
options.D: a bottleneck effect.

questions.explanation: Antigenic shift is a sudden major change caused by swapping gene segments between strains, which can cause pandemics. Option A is tempting, but drift is the slow build-up of small mutations.

questions.prompt: Which action would most directly break the transmission of a mosquito-borne zoonosis?

options.B: Draining standing water where mosquitoes breed
options.C: Reducing the incubation period of the pathogen
options.D: Testing people for antibodies after recovery

questions.explanation: Removing breeding sites reduces the number of vectors that carry the pathogen between hosts. Option A is tempting, but antibiotics do not stop mosquitoes spreading the pathogen, and many such diseases are viral.

questions.prompt: Which statement about genetic drift is correct?

options.A: It always increases the frequency of advantageous alleles.
options.B: It has its largest effect in very large populations.
options.C: It is the source of new alleles.
options.D: It is a random change in allele frequencies and can cause alleles to be lost.

questions.explanation: Drift is chance-driven, can fix or lose alleles and is strongest in small populations. Option A describes natural selection, and option C describes mutation.

questions.prompt: Dog breeds show huge variation in size and shape. The process mainly responsible is

options.A: selective breeding, where humans act as the selection pressure.
options.C: gene flow between wolf populations.
options.D: sympatric speciation.

questions.explanation: Humans chose which dogs bred, changing allele frequencies quickly. Option B is tempting, but the selection pressure was human choice, not survival in the wild. All breeds are still one species, so speciation has not occurred.

questions.prompt: A new plant species forms in a single generation when a hybrid's chromosome number doubles. This is

options.C: allopatric speciation by geographic isolation.
options.D: genetic drift.

questions.explanation: Polyploidy can make offspring instantly unable to breed with the parent species while living in the same area, so it is sympatric. Option A is tempting, but no geographical barrier is involved.

questions.prompt: In undisturbed sedimentary rock, fossil X is found in a layer below fossil Y. Which conclusion is valid?

options.C: X is 1 million years older than Y.
options.D: X is the direct ancestor of Y.

questions.explanation: By the law of superposition, lower layers were laid down first, so X is older. Option C is wrong because relative dating gives order, not ages in years. Option D is not supported; position does not prove ancestry.

questions.prompt: The wings of a bat and the wings of an insect are best described as

options.C: analogous structures, showing convergent evolution.
options.D: transitional features.

questions.explanation: Both are used for flight but have completely different structures and origins, so they are analogous. Option A is tempting because both are wings, but homologous structures share an underlying structure from a common ancestor.

questions.prompt: On a phylogenetic tree, species W and X share a node that is more recent than the node they share with species Y. This means

options.A: Y is the ancestor of W and X.
options.C: Y is more advanced than W and X.
options.D: W and X are more closely related to each other than either is to Y.

questions.explanation: The most recent shared node shows the closest relationship. Option A is tempting, but tips on a tree are living (or terminal) species, not ancestors; ancestors are at the nodes.

questions.prompt: Mitochondrial DNA evidence supports an African origin of modern humans. A key reason mtDNA is useful for this is that it

options.A: is inherited from both parents equally.
options.B: is inherited from the mother and does not recombine.
options.C: never mutates.
options.D: is found only in fossils.

questions.explanation: mtDNA passes down the maternal line without recombination, so differences build up only by mutation and can be traced back. Option C is wrong; mtDNA mutates relatively quickly, which is why it is useful for comparing closely related groups.

questions.prompt: A student tests the effect of temperature on the growth of bacteria on agar plates. Which is a controlled variable?

options.B: The diameter of bacterial colonies after 48 hours
options.C: The type and volume of agar in each plate
options.D: The number of colonies that grow

questions.explanation: The agar type and volume must be kept the same so only temperature changes. Option A is the independent variable, and options B and D are possible dependent variables.
